summary: Describes a procedure for mapping between Service Location Protocol (SLP) service advertisements and LDAP descriptions of services. It helps the two directory-style systems share service information.

eli5.summary: Two systems keep lists of available services in different formats. This is a translation guide between the lists.

questions: convert ldap schema to slp template
how to map service types between protocols
subtitle: Procedures for translating between two directory systems.

tldr.problem: Two important directory protocols, SLP and LDAP, store service information in different formats. Organizations need to use both systems together without maintaining duplicate information.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines procedures for mapping service attributes and schema between SLP service type templates and LDAP directory schema definitions, including how to represent SLP advertisements in LDAP directories.
tldr.outcome: The mapping is mostly straightforward when moving from simple SLP templates to LDAP, but the reverse is more complex if LDAP uses advanced ASN.1 types. Following these conventions allows SLP directory agents to back into LDAP servers.

today: RFC 2926 is an Informational RFC from 2000. It established conventions for translating between two directory protocols that were both deployed at the time. Modern deployments favour LDAP or other directory systems, but these mappings remain useful for legacy system interoperability.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Service Location Protocol (SLP) and Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) are both directory systems for finding network services. SLP uses simple text templates to define service types and their attributes, while LDAP uses schema written in a subset of ASN.1 notation. When both systems are deployed in the same network, interoperability becomes important.

This RFC creates mappings between the two systems. The goal is to let SLP directory agents (DAs) use LDAP directory servers as a backend store, so services registered in one system propagate easily to the other.
sections.eli5: Think of two libraries that catalog books differently. One uses simple checklists (SLP), the other uses detailed index cards (LDAP). This document explains how to translate one format into the other.

sections.title: Mapping SLP Templates to LDAP Schema
sections.content:
SLP templates are string-based and human-readable. They define a service type (like service:printer:lpr) with a version number, a description, and a list of attributes. Each attribute has a type (integer, string, boolean, or opaque), optional flags (like multi-valued or optional), and allowed values.

To convert a template to LDAP, the service type name becomes an LDAP object class name. Colons and periods become hyphens (so service:printer:lpr becomes service-printer-lpr). Attribute types map directly: SLP integers become LDAP INTEGER, strings become Directory String, booleans become BOOLEAN, and opaque becomes OCTET STRING.

Flags that LDAP cannot express (like the literal flag or explicit matching flag) are stored in the DESC field of the LDAP schema as comments. This preserves the information if the schema is converted back to a template later.
sections.eli5: Each service type becomes a class. Each attribute becomes a field. Simple types map directly. Complex things get written as notes in the description so they are not lost.

sections.title: Mapping LDAP Schema to SLP Templates
sections.content:
The reverse mapping is more complex. LDAP supports 33 attribute syntaxes (many based on ASN.1), while SLP has only four types: integer, string, boolean, and opaque. Most simple LDAP types map well: LDAP INTEGER becomes SLP integer, BOOLEAN becomes SLP boolean, and Directory String becomes SLP string. Audio, Certificate, and JPEG become opaque.

Complex ASN.1 types require encoding. Enumerations become SLP strings with allowed values listed. Object identifiers become strings. Real numbers (floating point) become strings. ASN.1 types that do not map cleanly are encoded as strings or opaque, with the original type recorded in the template comments.

If arbitrary complex ASN.1 types occur in the schema, conversion may be impossible.
sections.eli5: Translating backwards is harder because LDAP knows more types. Simple ones convert fine. Complicated ones have to be squeezed into one of four types and described in comments.

sections.title: Representing Service Advertisements in LDAP
sections.content:
For full interoperability, the RFC recommends how to store SLP service advertisements in an LDAP directory. Each service advertisement becomes an LDAP entry with a labeledURI attribute holding the service URL. This attribute is also used as the relative distinguished name (RDN), the part of the directory path that identifies the entry.

Services should be stored under ou=service below the domain object. For example, a printer service service:lpr://printsrv/queue1 in the domain foobar.com has the distinguished name labeledURI=service:lpr://printsrv/queue1,ou=service,dc=foobar,dc=com.

Service advertisements in SLP have a lease time. LDAP servers supporting dynamic directory services can extend the service advertisement entry with the dynamicObject class to allow entries to time out automatically.
sections.eli5: Services are stored as entries in the directory with their URL as the identifier. They live under a special folder called 'service' so they are easy to find.

sections.title: Internationalization Considerations
sections.content:
SLP specifies that every service advertisement carries an RFC 1766 language code. In LDAP, language codes are appended to attribute names with a semicolon, for example address;lang-de for German. LDAP servers that do not understand language tags treat them as unrecognized attributes.

If the service advertisement is in the default locale (English, no dialect), the language code need not be appended. When querying LDAP, RFC 2596 specifies that all matching entries are returned (including those with language tags) without requiring the tags in the query itself.
sections.eli5: Different languages are marked with language tags. The system can find services in your language without needing special queries.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SLP supports authenticators (digital signatures) on service URLs and attribute lists. When service advertisements are stored in LDAP, these authenticators are preserved as attributes. SLP directory agents that use LDAP as a backend and implement SLP authentication MUST use LDAP authentication to ensure the entries are secure.

LDAP clients querying the directory should use LDAP authentication to verify they are connecting to a secure server.
sections.eli5: When using LDAP to store signed services, use LDAP's security to protect the signatures.
